name: Deep Stone
lede: Deep Stone is a darker, more golden reading of [[stone]], recorded in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, plate 13 L 7.

sections.title: One chip, several names
sections.body:
The name follows the library's modifier grammar, *deep* plus [[stone]], and Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places the exact chip on plate 13 L 7 [1]. Their dictionary gives the same hex to three older names: Isabella, first recorded in 1601, Titiens, from 1892, and Samovar, from 1925, all on neighboring plates [1]. The books consulted here do not explain why later editors chose "stone" and "deep" over any of the three.

Its closest look-alike on file is [[pinchbeck-brown]], about 2.6 units off, with [[chamoline]] and [[sand-brown]] a little further out [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 7.74% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (1,841 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 1,477 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 93% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1300s, present in 20.7% of the 251 paintings we have from that decade (52 paintings), 3.2 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in 62% of its 1,477 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. Its most devoted painter is Fritz Thomsen, present in 6 of 18 works here, 5.7x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 6.9x) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1200, 730 years before the name's 1930 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
